name: Cardinal Determinative

dimensions.form: Basic (0-99) or magnitude determinative; no number inflection
dimensions.meaning: Supplies a cardinal value. Interpretation as an exact total or as a lower boundary depends on context.
dimensions.function: Heads DPs functioning as determiners, factors, or fused heads
dimensions.distribution: Determiner in NP; factor in magnitude phrases; fused determiner-head

1.definition: Cardinal numerative that can determine a nominal by giving a numerical value

examples.form: The building has [one thousand twenty-four] rooms.

constraints.description: Functions as determiner in NP structure; can appear as fused head (e.g., "I bought three").

projection.target: A cardinal determiner in thirty copies can alternate with some copies. In two hundred, two is internal to the numerative and can coexist with an external determiner in a two hundred, on the token reading.
projection.evidence: Reynolds uses coexistence with an external determiner to distinguish determiner function from multiplicative modification.

curious.title: Number words before nouns
curious.summary: A number word such as three or twenty-six can come before a noun and say how many there are.
curious.body: In I saw three cats, the word three tells us how many cats. Longer numbers work the same way: twenty-six students, or one thousand twenty-four rooms. The number comes at the front of the noun phrase and supplies a value. A number word can also stand in for the whole noun phrase when the noun is understood, as in I bought three. And whether a number means exactly that many or at least that many depends on the context.

examples.text: The building has [one thousand twenty-four] rooms.

curious.try: Say I bought three and then I bought three cats. Is the number doing the same job in both?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining that a cardinal word can serve as a determiner in a noun phrase, and that the same word can also stand alone for the whole noun phrase.
teacher.explain: Cardinal words such as three, twenty-six and one thousand twenty-four are determinatives (a word category) that serve as determiners (a function) in a noun phrase. They supply a numerical value and have no number inflection. A cardinal can also be a fused determiner-head, standing for the whole noun phrase, as in I bought three. In two hundred, the first word is a factor in the magnitude phrase rather than a determiner of the noun. Whether a cardinal gives an exact total or a lower boundary depends on context.
teacher.terms: Cardinal number or numeral: the traditional names. This dictionary says cardinal determinative for the word and determiner for the function. Numerative is the dictionary's own word for number words and phrases.

examples.text: The building has [one thousand twenty-four] rooms.

contrasts.note: Three is a determiner in the noun phrase three cats.

watch_for: A learner might take three to mean exactly three cats in every context, when context decides between an exact total and a lower boundary.
A learner might treat three in I bought three as a different kind of word from three in three cats.
A learner might expect a number word that determines a noun to take a plural ending, though cardinal determinatives have no number inflection.
teacher.activity: Give students short texts with number words. They underline each number and mark whether a noun follows it (three cats) or whether it stands alone (I bought three).

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.summary no longer says a number word before a noun is always a determiner (the entry distinguishes factors such as two in two hundred).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Cardinal Determinative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/cardinal-determinative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
